title: implement set_values for GaussLobatto and RadauPS phases
body:
set_values is the complement to get_values.  Given a continuous time-series of data, interpolate as necessary and insert into the appropriate state/control values.

set_values should remove the need for the user directly calling phase.interpolate, and therefore has to support a similar option set (xs, ys, interpolation kind). Signature should be

`phase.set_values(name, values, units=None, interp=None, interp_xs=None)`

`name` is the dymos variable name, where internally we check to see if it is  a time, state, control, or ODE variable.

`values` are the values to be assigned.

`units` are the units in which we are assigning the variable.  Internally the appropriate unit conversion will occur.

`interp` is the type of interpolation to perform on the given values.  Default should be None, which will raise an error if the given values aren't of the correct length.  

`interp_xs` are the time/independent variable values to use, equivalent to the `xs` argument to phase.interpolate.  If interp is `None` or `'linear'` then xs are not necessary, otherwise an error should be raised in its absence.

* Removed dynamic option from controls. All controls are dynamic, and static controls should now be implemented as design parameters.
* ControlRateComp changed to ControlInterpComp, and is now responsible for providing interpolated values of the controls at all nodes.
* Controls specified as inputs to ControlInterpComp are specified at the the 'control_input' subset, which accounts for compressed transcription, if present.  Even non-optimal, externally connected controls are now to be provided at the 'control_input' subset.
* RadauPS phase controls are now defined at the left n-1 nodes of the phase (not including the right endpoint).  Enforcing value continuity in this case is now a nonlinear constraint, as is the case for rate and rate2 continuity.

* ContinuityComp has been replaced with two transcription-specific versions, GaussLobattoContinuityComp and RadauPSContinuityComp.  This enabled the removal of transcription checking from the component, providing cleaner code.

title: Trajectory Objects
body:
Trajectory objects are Groups which serve to organize a set of one or more phases.

Each Trajectory group consists of two primary subsystems:
- phases
    A ParallelGroup within the Trajectory that can hold each phase, and potentially evaluate them in parallel
- linkages
    A PhaseLinkageComp that manages all of the linkage constraints between phases

Trajectory objects as currently envisioned have the following primary methods:
- `add_phase(phase_name, phase_object, **kwargs)`

    Phases are added to a trajectory with an `add_phase` method.  Functionally, it's very similar to the `add_subsystem` method of ParallelGroup.  Phases are cached in an internal dictionary `_phases`, and then actually added to the phases subgroup during setup.

- `link_phase(phases, vars=['*'], locs=('++', '--'))`
    Trajectory objects provide a `link_phases` method that provides an ordering of phases in the trajectory.  The goal of `link_phases` is to make common phase linkages (sequential) trivial, and complicated phase linkages (parallel, multiple branches, etc) tractable.

    Argument `phases` provides a series of two or more phases that follow one another in sequence.  Argument `vars` provides the name of the time, state, controls, or control rates to be linked.  Providing the value '*' in the list here will imply that time and all *common* state variables between the phases are to be linked.  Providing a tuple-pair as one of the elements in vars allows variables of different names to be connected across phases.

    Finally `locs` provides the location of the connection for each pair of phases in the given sequence, using the `--`, `-+`, `+-`, `++` convention for states and controls. 

    Ultimately link_phases should probably provide the same functionality as OTIS's global constraints, where any variables can be connected between two phases.

- `simulate(times, parallel=True)`
    Simulate each phase in the trajectory, returning the results of each simulation in a dictionary.  Use python's multiprocessing module to simulate each phase simultaneously when possible, to improve performance.

- `get_values(var, phases=None, nodes='all', flat=False)`
    Return the values of a given variable at the given nodes through the given sequence of phases in the trajectory.  Omitting phases returns the variable in all phases.  If not present, return nan for each node in the phase.  Might have to think about how we treat variables which may have different shapes in different phases, since plotting a 3-vector from various phases, and then just a 1-vector of nans from a phase where the variable is not present.  If flat, rather than returning a dictionary, return a continuous array across phases.

title: Trajectories support design parameters
body:
This enhancement allows trajectories to own design parameters.  The design parameters can then be connected to each phase within the trajectory.  

Syntax:
`trajectory.add_design_parameter(name, val, units=None, targets=None, opt=True, input=False, lower, upper, adder, scaler, ref0, ref)`

All options are the same for the phase `add_design_parameter` method except for targets.  If given, targets is a dictionary that maps each phase name to the ODE parameter name to which it is being connected.  This allows a single design parameter at the trajectory level to be connected to variables which may have different names in different phases.  If targets is None, assume that the given name is also the name of the target parameter in each phase.

title: AnalyticPhase
body:
Define an AnalyticPhase for which the solution to the ODE is known analytically.  Rather than taking an ODE, take a system that provides a solution for any time.

This would be useful to have on some of the project's we're currently working, so I'm bumping the priority up.

For the initial cut, we need a new Phase called `AnalyticPhase` that inherits from`Phase` and overrides some of its methods.

## Handling states

In an analytic phase, states are really just outputs of the form `f(x0, t, p)`.
That is analytic phase will, at least initially, fundamentally just solve the IVP analytically, providing states just as any other output.
We'll maintain an official list of states for the sake of keeping things consistent with other phases in dymos when it comes to linking them together and stuff like that.

We will override the `set_state_options` method so that it doesn't have a `rate_src`, but instead has `val_src` - the output in the ODE that provides the value of the state at a given time.

## Handling controls

Initially there will be no support for controls in AnalyticPhase.
Attempting to add a control or polynomial control will raise an exception.
I'm not certain that there's any example where an ODE with dynamic controls has an analytic solution.

## TImeseries outputs

Timeseries outputs will still be provided in the form `phasename.timeseries.*` in order to be consistent with other phases, to support constraints and linkages.

## Transcriptions

I don't think it makes sense that AnalyticPhases have transcriptions.  In this case we're not really converting an infinite-dimensional optimal control problem to a discrete optimization problem.

Still, the mechanisms in dymos dictate that the transcription helps to setup/configure the phase, so we'll have an AnalyticTranscription that will just automatically be associated with the AnalyticPhase.

The next question is, where do the nodes go?
For this initial cut I think it makes sense that AnalyticPhase has a `num_nodes` option and provides output nodes by using the formula `np.linspace(t_initial, t_initial + t_duration, num_nodes)`.

## Constraints

We should still support path and boundary constraints as we do with the other Phase/transcription types.
From a control viewpoint, this phase is similar to `ExplicitShooting`, in that it fundamentally is governed by values of the initial states, parameters, initial time and duration.

## Possible example cases

1. Propagating a 2-body orbit using f and g series.  Example [here](https://gereshes.com/2018/06/25/lagrange-fg-solution-the-2-body-problem/)

2. Propagate some simple ODE, such as the one [here](https://math.okstate.edu/people/yqwang/teaching/math4513_fall11/Notes/rungekutta.pdf)

body:
Options `fixed_initial` and `fixed_final` are not sufficient to determine the direction of integration of each variable.  Change the current state option `direction` (used only by RungeKuttaPhase at the moment) to `time_direction`.

Options `connected_initial` and `connected_final` specify that either the initial state value or final state value is to be connected to another output.

If options `fixed_initial` or `fixed_final` are True, then the optimizer owns those values and the initial/final values are *not* design variables.  If they are fixed then they cannot be connected.  `fixed_final` cannot be used in forward shooting (`time_direction = 1`) and option `fixed_initial` cannot be used with backward shooting `time_direction = -1`

If options `fixed_initial` or `fixed_final` are False, and the respective `connect_initial` or `connect_final` is False, then the initial/final value is governed by the optimizer as a design variable.

There are various combinations of these options that are invalid that need to be checked.

title: PolynomialControls
body:
Adds "polynomial controls" to Dymos.

Polynomial controls are based on polynomials that span the entire Phase, rather than segment by segment.  To add a polynomial control to a phase, use `phase.add_polynomial_control(name, order, ...)` where order is the order of the polynomial which will provide the control values.  For instance, to provide a linear control time history over the entire phase specify:

`phase.add_polynomial_control('u', order=1)`

The control values are input at the LGL nodes in _phase_ tau space, so a first order polynomial like that above will be defined by values at [-1, 1] (the beginning and end) of the phase.

Polynomial controls are provided by a self-contained group which houses both the indep var comp and the interpolation component which maps values from the input nodes `phase.polynomial_controls:u` to the values, rates, and second derivatives at _all_ nodes:
values:  `phase.polynomial_control_values:u`
first derivative:  `phase.polynomial_control_rates:u_rate`
second derivative:  `phase.polynomial_control_values:u_rate2`

Polynomial controls are added to the timeseries output of the phase classes.  
values:  `phase.timeseries.polynomial_control_values:u`
first derivative:  `phase.timeseries.polynomial_control_rates:u_rate`
second derivative:  `phase.timeseries.polynomial_control_values:u_rate2`

Note this PR does not implement polynomial controls in SimulationPhases, which will be addressed by a future issue.

Resolves #123

title: User can specify boundary constraints on non-scalar variables
body:
With the addition of shooting phases, terminal boundary constraints on states can only be accomplished with nonlinear boundary constraints (`fix_final` is not a valid option).

If we have vector state variables (or other variables to be boundary-constrained), the current boundary constraint comp is not capable of handling them.

If the constrained variable is not an ODE output, we should be able to figure out its shape from time, state, control, or design/input parameter options.  If it is an ODE output, the user will need to specify its shape in the add_boundary_constraint arguments.

Add `indices` as an argument to add_boundary_constraint.  If `indices=None`, then the boundary constraint should apply to all elements and lower/upper/equals should have the same shape as the constrained variable, or be a scalar.  If provided, then indices should provide a sequence of indices into the constrained variable to which the constraint applies.  In this case, lower/upper/equals should be supplied as a scalar or *as a flattened list of the bounds on each index in the order specified*.

For instance, if we have a 3D position vector `[x, y, z]` and wish to apply boundary constraints on only the first and last elements:

`phase.add_boundary_constraint('pos', loc='final', indices=[0, 2], lower=[x_lb, z_lb], upper=[x_ub, z_ub])`

title: Adding path constraints, boundary contraints, and objective adds them to timeseries outputs.

title: Separate transcription from phase
body:
### Draft

In order to make defining phase classes easier, the transcription should be separated from Phase.

Class PhaseBase will be replaced by class Phase(Group) and the setup stack will largely be unchanged.  All of the setup methods in the setup stack that are currently implemented in Phase subclasses will instead by implemented in the Transcriptions.  These setup methods in transcription will accept a phase object as an argument, and add the appropriate systems/etc.

So for instance, currently for the brachistochrone we typically do this:
```
    phase = Phase('gauss-lobatto',
                  ode_class=BrachistochroneODE,
                  num_segments=10,
                  transcription_order=3,
                  compressed=True)
```
which will change to 

```
    phase = Phase(ode_class=BrachistochroneODE,
                  transcription=GaussLobatto(num_segments=10,
                                             transcription_order=3,
                                             compressed=True))
```

A new `transcriptions` subpackage in the dymos directory will hold the transcriptions:
- TranscriptionBase
- CollocationTranscriptionBase
    - GaussLobatto
    - Radau
- RungeKutta
- SolveIVP

title: Allow user to add states/controls/parameters as timeseries outputs.
body:
Currently states, controls, and parameters are have `states:`, `controls:`, `design_parameters:`, `input_parameters:`, etc. prepended to their names in the timeseries outputs.

While this is useful for understanding the structure of a problem, it would be more convenient in some cases if we allowed them to be explicitly added as additional timeseries outputs.  For instance, in a trajectory where altitude is a state in one phase but a control in another, and we want to plot the entire history, the naming would be more uniform.

Currently we simply ignore any request by the user to add these to the timeseries output, since they're included by default.  This change will include them in duplicate, once with a prepended name, but once with their bare name.

title: Trajectory Parameter Cleanup
body:
A trajectory parameter named `foo` by default will be connected to targets [`foo`] in each phase.  The `_setup_input_parameters` and `_setup_design_parameters` methods on Trajectory will determine if `foo` is a decorated ODE parameter in each phase and handle it appropriately.

`add_input_parameter` arguments `targets` and `target_params` will be replaced by `custom_targets` which will override the default with a path (string) or list of paths.

title: Trajectory Parameter Cleanup
body:
### Summary

Specifying targets for trajectory design and input parameters within each constituent phase is now done with the `custom_targets` argument to `Trajectory.add_design_parameter` and `Trajectory.add_input_parameter`.

- If `custom_targets` is not specified, the target of a trajectory parameter in each phase is assumed to be a decorated ODE parameter of the same name.
- Otherwise `custom_targets` is given as a dictionary keyed by phase name with the following rules
  - If the value associated with the name of a phase is `None`, the trajectory parameter is _not_ connected to that phase.
  - If the value associated with the name of a phase is a string, the trajectory parameter is connected to a decorated ODE parameter of the same name within the phase.
  - If the value associated with the name of a phase is a list, it is assumed to be a list of targets relative to the ODE within that phase.

### Related Issues

- Resolves #185 

### Status

- [x] Ready for merge

### Backwards incompatibilities

Removes `targets` and `target_params` from `Trajectory.add_design_parameter` and `Trajectory.add_input_parameter`, replaced by `custom_targets`.

### New Dependencies

None

Allow two phases with different grids and different ODEs to be run over the same timespan.  This allows states and controls "owned" by one phase to be passed as inputs to another phase.

title: Deprecate ODE decorators
body:
ODE decorators were originally intended to remove the need to repeatedly declare the same information over and over again for a phase.  In certain context, like repeatedly testing simple ODEs like the brachistochrone this makes a lot of sense.

In use however, the ODE systems we develop turn out to not be used as the top-level ODE all that often.  Flight dynamics equations of motion for an aircraft, for example, are typically only a part of the overall ODE along with thermal dynamic equations.

The static nature of decorators makes them problematic for creating ODEs programmatically.  If we require the states/controls/parameters to be declared at the phase level then we can define them at setup (and do so programmatically).  This also gets us back to having one preferred way of doing it.

If a state/time/parameter has many targets in the ODE, the user can make things simpler by promoting these up to the top level of the ODE, thus only one target will need to be defined for that variable.

body:
### Summary

Argument `custom_targets` for trajectory design and input parameters is now just `targets`, with the following rules:

*  If `targets` is `None` the trajectory design or input parameter will be connected to the phase input parameter of the same name in each phase, if it exists (otherwise it is not connected to that phase).

*  Otherwise targets should be specified as a dictionary. And the behavior depends on the value associated with each phase name:

    * If the phase name is not in the given dictionary, attempt to connect to an existing input parameter of the same name in that phase.

    * If the associated value is None, explicitly omit a connection to that phase.

    * If the associated value is a string, connect to an existing input parameter whose name is given by the string in that phase.

    * If the associated value is a Sequence, create an input parameter in that phase connected to the ODE targets given by the Sequence.

Argument `custom_targets` will throw a DeprecationWarning and be treated as `targets`, with the behavior above.

### Related Issues

- Resolves #230 

### Status

title: Allow `add_state` to be called in the setup method of Phase
body:
Recent updates to OpenMDAO allow inputs/outputs to be specified in configure.
Because of this, we can now in theory associate state variables to be integrated with an ODE system.  However, since we want to maintain ODE's as pure OpenMDAO systems with no special Dymos features, we can achieve similar benefits by using a subclassed Phase.

Given an ODE class MyODE, we can implement a Phase that always uses that given ODE as:

```
class MyPhase(dm.Phase):

    def __init__(self, transcription):
        super(transcription, ode_class=MyODE)

    def setup(self):
        self.add_state('x', targets=['target.path.in.ode'], rate_source='rate.source.path.in.ode', units='m')
```

Then we can instantiate MyPhase and avoid having to repeat the target, rate source, and possibly units information each time we declare MyPhase.  This removes the current DRY principle issue in Dymos where states need to be added with target/source information even though this is generally can be set once and never changed again.

title: Include autoscaling capability
body:
### Summary of Issue

Merge autoscaling capability into dymos.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

ISO Scaling and PJRN scaling techniques originally published by Sagliano et. al. (https://elib.dlr.de/93327/1/Performance_analysis_of_linear_and_nonlinear_techniques.pdf) and tested with Dymos by Harvey Weyandt (https://github.com/robfalck/autoscaling) should be merged into the Dymos codebase.

The `dymos.run_problem` function, which is currently used to facilitate grid refinement of a Dymos problem, should be expanded to include automatic scaling.

The proposed signature of `run_problem`is:

```
def run_problem(problem, refine=False, refine_iteration_limit=10, autoscaling=None)
```

By default, `autoscaling=None` attempts no automatic scaling of the problem.  Other possible values for autoscaling are `'pjrn'` or `'iso'` (case insensitive).

The behavior of run_problem should change such that, `if autoscaling is not None`, then run_model is invoked to finalize setup, followed by a calculation of the necessary inputs for the autoscaling.  Once complete, the driver will be run with the appropriate scaling and, if necessary, the refinement algorithm will proceed as it currently does.

### Example

For example, the current implementation for the brachistochrone at https://github.com/robfalck/autoscaling/blob/master/autoscaling/examples/brach/opt_brach.py should now be the same, but the lines:

```
    with open('total_jac_info.pickle', 'rb') as file:
        jac = pickle.load(file)
    with open('lower_bounds_info.pickle', 'rb') as file:
        lbs = pickle.load(file)
    with open('upper_bounds_info.pickle', 'rb') as file:
        ubs = pickle.load(file)

    sc = PJRNScaler(jac, lbs, ubs)
    autoscale(prob, autoscaler=sc)
    prob.run_driver()
```

will be replaced with

```
    dm.run_problem(autoscale='PJRN')
```

We should also do whatever necessary to remove the need to pickle the jacobian and bounds information.

N/A

title: Dymos command line interface
body:
### Summary of Issue

Add a command line interface workflow for Dymos.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

A CLI will be added for Dymos to improve the workflow.
Like the OpenMDAO CLI, it will use post-final-setup hooks to obtain a problem instance from a given python file.

Initially, the syntax of the CLI will be as follows:

```
dymos --simulate --no_solve --solution=<solution_record.sql> --reset_grid --refine_limit=0 <problem_definition_file.py>
```

Where:
```
problem_definition_file.py - The python file in which the problem to be run is defined.
--simulate - If given, perform simulation after solving the problem
--no_solve - If given, do not run the driver on the problem (simulate only)
--solution - A previous solution record file (or explicit simulation record file) from which the initial guess should be loaded.
--reset_grid - If given, reset the grid to the specs given in the problem definition instead of the grid associated with the loaded solution.
--refine_limit=0 - The number of passes through the grid refinement algorithm to use.
```

### Example

For instance, if we define the brachistochrone problem in `brachistochrone.py` then we could generate an explicit guess based on the default control and design parameter values with

```
dymos --simulate --no_solve brachistochrone.py
```

This would generate an explicit simulation record file named `brachistochrone_sim.sql`

We could then bootstrap the solution using that explicit simulation as the initial guess and use 3 passes of the grid refinement algorithm with:

```
dymos brachistochrone.py --solution=brachistochrone_sim.sql --refine_limit=3
```

This would save the new optimized and refined solution in a file named `brachistochrone_solution.sql`.

title: Phase linking doesn't pick up units if variables are input or design parameters.
body:
### Summary of Issue

When linking phases together, the units of the linked variables aren't always correct.

### Issue Type

- [x] Bug
- [ ] Enhancement

### Description

When setting up linked variables, units aren't extracted if the variable exists as an input or design parameter in the first phase of the linkage.  The offending code starts at line 365 of trajectory.py:

```
            for var, options in _vars.items():
                if options['connected']:
                    # If this is a state, and we are linking it, we need to do some checks.
                    if var in p2_states:
                        # Trajectory linkage modifies these options in connected states.
                        p2.add_state(var, connected_initial=True)
                    elif var == 'time':
                        p2.set_time_options(input_initial=True)
                else:
                    vars_to_constrain.append(var)
                    if var in p1_states:
                        units_map[var] = p1.state_options[var]['units']
                        shape_map[var] = p1.state_options[var]['shape']
                    elif var in p1_controls:
                        units_map[var] = p1.control_options[var]['units']
                        shape_map[var] = p1.control_options[var]['shape']
                    elif var == 'time':
                        units_map[var] = p1.time_options['units']
                        shape_map[var] = (1,)
                    else:
                        units_map[var] = None
                        shape_map[var] = (1,)
```

### Example

As a result, when linking a design parameter in the first phase to a state in the second phase, one might see an error like this:

```
Output 'phases.take_off.design_parameters:h' with units of 'ft' is connected to input 'linkages.take_off|climb_h:lhs' which has no units.
```

### Environment

Operating System: OS X 10.14.6
Python environment: Anaconda Python 3.7.5

title: dymos.run_problem should allow a previous solution to be interpolated onto a different grid
body:
### Summary of Issue

Allow the user to "reset" the grid when using a restart file.  The solution from a previous run on some grid will be reinterpolated onto the grid as originally defined for the problem.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

When a dymos problem is run and grid refinement is enabled, the solution at which it arrives will likely be on a different grid than that originally defined for the problem.  While refined solutions are more accurate, sometimes it is desirable to reduce the size of the grid -- for instance, when changing an input and needing to reconverge a solution, a simpler grid will often converge to the solution sooner.  This "moved" solution can then be cleaned up with grid refinement that starts from the simple grid.

### Example

Running from the command line, one might run a problem with a restart file wherein the restart file contains a more complex grid (more segments and/or higher order segments, leading to more variables and constraints in the problem).

```
dymos problem_definition.py --solution=previous_solution.sql --reset_grid
```

to use that original simplified grid as a starting point for further refinement, one would invoke:

```
dymos problem_definition.py --solution=previous_solution.sql --reset_grid --refine_limit=10
```

### Environment

N/A

title: Using wildcard in phase linkages yields randomness
body:
### Summary of Issue
When linking multiple phases into a trajectory, using a wildcard for variables `traj.link_phases(vars=['*'])` seems to result in a random order of the linkage constraints. This randomness could be an issue in terms of the reproducibility of optimization.   

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

Since the order of the linkage constraint would be random with the wildcard, the Jacobian (of constraints wrt variables) structure would be different every time one runs the same script. As a result some optimizers would behave differently, even if the set of variables, constraints, and objective is identical. Depending on the complication of the problem, one may get different converged solutions, or convergence failure, after running the identical script multiple times.   
I'm wondering it would be great if you could remove the randomness coming from the wildcard entry, or add this behavior in the document. 

### Example

Running the [multi-phase cannonball example](https://openmdao.github.io/dymos/examples/multi_phase_cannonball.html) produces (slightly) different convergence history each time. I observed this behavior with SNOPT and SLSQP wrapped by pyoptsparse driver.  
By specifying all the variables to be connected explicitly instead of the wildcard, i.e. 
```python
# traj.link_phases(phases=['ascent', 'descent'], vars=['*'])
traj.link_phases(phases=['ascent', 'descent'], vars=['time', 'v', 'gam', 'r', 'h'])
```
then optimization history becomes reproducable. 

Thank you,
Shugo

### Summary of Issue

Add a new argument `include_timeseries=True/False` to `add_input_parameter` and `add_design_parameter`, to allow static parameters to be omitted from the timeseries output when they are large.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

Originally we made the design decision to include static parameters (design parameters and input parameters) in the timeseries output by default for the sake of consistency, and to allow timeseries to be a single source of any relevant variable which the user wanted to plot.

However, when input and design parameters have a high number of dimensions, this results in a lot of wasted space.  This issue gives the user the option of omitting input and design parameters from the timeseries output with an argument to `add_design_parameter` and `add_input_parameter`.

The new option, `include_timeseries` will be True by default, but a value of False will allow the user to prevent it from being sent to the timeseries output.

title: Improve efficiency of interpolation routines
body:
### Summary of Issue

The state and control interpolation routines are based upon the multiplication of constant matrices by the state or control vectors.  Phases with many segments, these matrices can be significantly sparse.  This issue involves changing these matrices to scipy sparse CSR matrices to reduce the memory footprint of these components, as well as potentially buying some performance boosts in `compute_partials`.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

The generalization of the LGL and LGR schemes interpolates states with up to 4 matrices:  [A]_i, [B]_i, [A]_d, and [B]_d, and controls with [L] and [D]  Currently these matrices are dense numpy arrays, but in phases with many segments they are significantly sparse.

They will be changed to scipy sparse CSR format matrices to improve overall performance.

title: Sparsity update
body:
### Summary

Cleanup of state and control interpolation to utilize sparse matrices via scipy.sparse.

Since theres significant sparsity in the state and control interpolation matrices, especially as the number of segments increases, this PR changes the state and control interpolation components to store components used for interpolation and partial evaluation as sparse matrices.

In addition, the components now reshape N-dimension inputs such that each element is treated as its own state vector.  This allows dymos to operate on states and controls with a completely arbitrary number of dimensions (previously states were limited to 3 dimensions).

title: Serial phase execution
body:
### Summary of Issue

Allow user to specify that Trajectory phases subgroup is a standard `Group` rather than `ParallelGroup`.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

Phases in a Trajectory are stored in a subgroup named `phases`.  This subgroup is a ParallelGroup, because in most operating modes, Phases are connected through constraints and they can be executed in Parallel.

In some cases it makes sense to force the phases to be run serially, like when there is some explicit connection (not constraint) linking one phase to the subsequent phase.

To support this, Trajectory will support a new option `parallel_phases` which will default to True (the current behavior).  When False, the `phases` subsystem should be created as a `Group()` rather than a `ParallelGroup()`.

The examples which use connected phases should use `parallel_phases=False` in the parent Trajectory objects.

title: Phase subgroups
body:
### Summary of Issue

Allow groups of phases to be added to trajectories.  These phases will be placed into subgroups which can contain their own solvers and other group-level properties.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

Currently, phases are added to a trajectory one phase at a time.  At times, certain phases in a trajectory will have circular dependencies requiring that they be run in their own Group.

Rather than forcing all phases to be run in this iterative group, this change will allow subgroups to be run in parallel with other phases.

### Example

Consider the following structure

```
Trajectory
    Phases
        Phase1
        Group
            Phase2
            Phase3
        Phase4
```

This would be accomplished by doing the following

traj.add_phase('phase1', phase1)
traj.add_phase(name=['phase2', 'phase3'], phase=[phase2, phase3], phase_add_kwargs=[kwargs2, kwargs3],  group_name='subgroup1', **kwargs)
traj.add_phase('phase4', phase4)

Proposed API:

A new method will be added to Trajectory that allows a group of phases to be added to the phases subgroup.  This group will be of class Group().  All phases within that group, and the group itself, will promote all inputs and outputs.

The existing API is:
```
trajectory.add_phase(name, phase, **kwargs)
```

The new API will be:
```
trajectory.add_phase(name, phase, phase_add_kwargs=None, group_name=None, kwargs**)
```

Here the use of `kwargs` will be deprecated in favor of `phase_add_kwargs`.

When adding multiple phases simultaneously:
- `name`, `phase`, (and `phase_add_kwargs` if not None) should have the same length.
-  If group_name is provided
    - The added phases will be put in a subgroup group_name

If group_name is provided, the add_phase method will return the Group to which the phases will be added during setup.  This group will need to be cached so that it can be added to phases during setup, but still available before that so properties like solvers can be set.

When a phase initial time or duration is specified from an external source (via the `input_initial` or `input_duration` options), calling phase.simulate() will raise the following error:

```
NameError: Phase (phase0): Attempted to connect from 't_initial' to 'segment_0.t_initial', but 't_initial' is an input. All connections must be from an output to an input.
```

In this case, `phase.t_initial` is an input so the connect statement in SolveIVPTranscription.setup_time is invalid:

```
        for i in range(num_seg):
            phase.connect('t_initial', 'segment_{0}.t_initial'.format(i))
            phase.connect('t_duration', 'segment_{0}.t_duration'.format(i))
```

In this case, the best way to resolve this is probably to just promote `segment{i}.t_initial` and `segment{i}.t_duration`.

### Example

An existing test in the repo has been modified to test this issue:
https://github.com/robfalck/dymos/blob/30eb93420d2982b857c17a86d18b770e9bbd8b5a/dymos/examples/double_integrator/test/test_double_integrator.py#L104

title: States, controls, and parameters targets should default to their name unless otherwise specified
body:
### Summary of Issue

States, controls, and parameters try to connect to inputs of their name in the ODE by default.  This would be a backwards incompatible change, since a target of `None` is different than a target of `_unspecified`.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

A common cause for error in Dymos is users forgetting to provide targets for states, controls, and parameters in a phase.  This change proposes that, if left "_unspecified", states, controls, and parameters will attempt to connect to a top level ODE input with the same name.

The current default behavior of None is to issue no connection (the ODE is independent output is independent of that given state).

To obtain the current default behavior, the user would have to explicitly provide `targets=None`, whereas the default `targets=_unspecified` will result in connections to the default input name.

Care will need to be taken on how we implement this in a deprecated way.

### Example

ODE output is not dependent on the value of x (for instance, vertical acceleration in a uniform rectilinear gravity field:
```
phase.add_state('x', targets=None, ...)
```

ODE input `x` is expecting to be connected to the value of state `x`:
```
phase.add_state('x', ...)
```

User explicitly provides a target for x:
```
phase.add_state('x', targets=['x'], ...)
```

title: Remove IndepVarComps for DesignParameters / Deprecate InputParameter
body:
### Summary of Issue

Parameter refactor: Update Design/Input Parameters to take advantage of OpenMDAO 3.2.0

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

- DesignParameters no longer need to have an IndepVarComp to provide their values.
- Design parameters/Input parameters will be combined into Parameters in Dymos 1.0.0
- Phase and Trajectory objects will now have an `add_parameter` method that supercedes both `add_design_parameter` and `add_input_parameter`.
- When `opt=False`, this should have the same functionality as InputParameters.
- If the parameter has `opt=True`, then `<path_to_phase>.parameters:<parameter_name>` should be a design variable for the optimization.

Implementation details:

- Targets of phase parameters should be promoted up to `<path_to_phase>.parameters:<parameter_name>` .
- If the parameter is dynamic (default), then the phase should use `set_input_defaults` to set the src_indices of the common phase level input (`<path_to_phase>.parameters:<parameter_name>`) such that the static parameter value is 'fanned' out to the targets.
- Phase and Trajectory add_design_parameter and add_input_parameter methods will deprecate with the message 'DesignParameters and InputParameters are being replaced by Parameters in Dymos 1.0.0.  Please use `add_parameter` or `set_parameter_options` to remove this deprecation warning.


### Example

The SSTO example documentation treats `thrust` as a non-optimized design parameter.
The the switch to `add_parameter` for this case is pretty trivial:

```
import unittest

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.switch_backend('Agg')
plt.style.use('ggplot')

from dymos.utils.doc_utils import save_for_docs


class TestDocSSTOEarth(unittest.TestCase):

    @save_for_docs
    def test_doc_ssto_earth(self):
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
        import openmdao.api as om
        from openmdao.utils.assert_utils import assert_near_equal
        import dymos as dm
        from dymos.examples.ssto.launch_vehicle_ode import LaunchVehicleODE

        #
        # Setup and solve the optimal control problem
        #
        p = om.Problem(model=om.Group())
        p.driver = om.pyOptSparseDriver()
        p.driver.declare_coloring()

        #
        # Initialize our Trajectory and Phase
        #
        traj = dm.Trajectory()

        phase = dm.Phase(ode_class=LaunchVehicleODE,
                         ode_init_kwargs={'central_body': 'earth'},
                         transcription=dm.GaussLobatto(num_segments=12, order=3, compressed=False))

        traj.add_phase('phase0', phase)
        p.model.add_subsystem('traj', traj)

        #
        # Set the options for the variables
        #
        phase.set_time_options(initial_bounds=(0, 0), duration_bounds=(10, 500))

        phase.add_state('x', fix_initial=True, ref=1.0E5, defect_ref=1.0,
                        rate_source='eom.xdot', units='m')
        phase.add_state('y', fix_initial=True, ref=1.0E5, defect_ref=1.0,
                        rate_source='eom.ydot', targets=['atmos.y'], units='m')
        phase.add_state('vx', fix_initial=True, ref=1.0E3, defect_ref=1.0,
                        rate_source='eom.vxdot', targets=['eom.vx'], units='m/s')
        phase.add_state('vy', fix_initial=True, ref=1.0E3, defect_ref=1.0,
                        rate_source='eom.vydot', targets=['eom.vy'], units='m/s')
        phase.add_state('m', fix_initial=True, ref=1.0E3, defect_ref=1.0,
                        rate_source='eom.mdot', targets=['eom.m'], units='kg')

        phase.add_control('theta', units='rad', lower=-1.57, upper=1.57, targets=['eom.theta'])
        phase.add_parameter('thrust', units='N', opt=False, val=1.0, targets=['eom.thrust'])

        #
        # Set the options for our constraints and objective
        #
        phase.add_boundary_constraint('y', loc='final', equals=1.85E5, linear=True)
        phase.add_boundary_constraint('vx', loc='final', equals=7796.6961, linear=True)
        phase.add_boundary_constraint('vy', loc='final', equals=0, linear=True)

        phase.add_objective('time', loc='final', scaler=0.01)

        p.model.linear_solver = om.DirectSolver()

        #
        # Setup and set initial values
        #
        p.setup(check=True)

        p.set_val('traj.phase0.t_initial', 0.0)
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.t_duration', 150.0)
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.states:x', phase.interpolate(ys=[0, 1.15E5], nodes='state_input'))
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.states:y', phase.interpolate(ys=[0, 1.85E5], nodes='state_input'))
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.states:vx', phase.interpolate(ys=[0, 7796.6961], nodes='state_input'))
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.states:vy', phase.interpolate(ys=[1.0E-6, 0], nodes='state_input'))
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.states:m', phase.interpolate(ys=[117000, 1163], nodes='state_input'))
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.controls:theta', phase.interpolate(ys=[1.5, -0.76], nodes='control_input'))
        p.set_val('traj.phase0.parameters:thrust', 2100000.0)

        #
        # Solve the Problem
        #
        dm.run_problem(p)

        #
        # Check the results.
        #
        assert_near_equal(p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.time')[-1], 143, tolerance=0.05)
        assert_near_equal(p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:y')[-1], 1.85E5, 1e-4)
        assert_near_equal(p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:vx')[-1], 7796.6961, 1e-4)
        assert_near_equal(p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:vy')[-1], 0, 1e-4)
        #
        # Get the explitly simulated results
        #
        exp_out = traj.simulate()

        #
        # Plot the results
        #
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=2, ncols=1, figsize=(10, 8))

        axes[0].plot(p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:x'),
                     p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:y'),
                     marker='o',
                     ms=4,
                     linestyle='None',
                     label='solution')

        axes[0].plot(exp_out.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:x'),
                     exp_out.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.states:y'),
                     marker=None,
                     linestyle='-',
                     label='simulation')

        axes[0].set_xlabel('range (m)')
        axes[0].set_ylabel('altitude (m)')
        axes[0].set_aspect('equal')

        axes[1].plot(p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.time'),
                     p.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.controls:theta'),
                     marker='o',
                     ms=4,
                     linestyle='None')

        axes[1].plot(exp_out.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.time'),
                     exp_out.get_val('traj.phase0.timeseries.controls:theta'),
                     linestyle='-',
                     marker=None)

        axes[1].set_xlabel('time (s)')
        axes[1].set_ylabel('theta (deg)')

        plt.suptitle('Single Stage to Orbit Solution Using Linear Tangent Guidance')
        fig.legend(loc='lower center', ncol=2)

        plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
```

title: Add release to bumpversion configuration
body:
### Summary of Issue

Dymos devs use [bump2version](https://github.com/c4urself/bump2version/) to automatically find and change references to the version of dymos when it is changed.  Currently a completely canonical {major}.{minor}.{patch} version system is used.

To distinguish the developmental master branch from releases, this will be changed to `{major}.{minor}.{patch}` for releases and `{major}.{minor}.{patch}-dev` for developmental versions.

This method will avoid issues that pip has with version ordering, making sure that version `{M}.{m}.{p}` always precedes `{M}.{m}.{p+1}-dev`.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

Details on how to accomplish this are [here](https://github.com/c4urself/bump2version/#configuration-file----part-specific-configuration), and that repo uses the desired behavior in its [.bumpversion.cfg file](https://github.com/c4urself/bump2version/blob/master/.bumpversion.cfg).:

### Example

Starting from `0.15.0`, issuing

`bump2version patch`

will increment the version to `0.15.1-dev`.

The dev tag will remain in place until a release is ready to be made, which is done by issuing

`bump2version release`

to obtain version `0.15.1` (or whatever the major, minor, patch numbers are at that point).

### Environment

N/A

title: Automatic target detection
body:
### Summary of Issue

The natural behavior of variables in the Dymos optimal control problem should be that they are connected to top-level ODE inputs of the same name, if present.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

If `targets` of a time, state, control, or parameter is left _unspecified_, Dymos should determine if the name of the variable is a **top-level** input to the ODE.  If so, it should automatically be connected.  If no such inputs are present, no target is connected (it must be done so manually in that case).

Variables of the same name, buried somewhere within the ODE, should not be be automatically connected.

The user can specify explicitly that the variable has no targets within the ODE (such is the case often with `time` or some state variables) by specifying `targets=None`.

This functionality relies on OpenMDAO issue OpenMDAO/OpenMDAO#1379

### Example

The brachistochrone quick start example offers a good demonstration where targets of state `v` and control `theta` have the same name as the state/control themselves:

```
        phase.add_state('v', fix_initial=True, fix_final=False, units='m/s', rate_source='vdot', targets=['v'])
        phase.add_control(name='theta', units='rad', lower=0, upper=np.pi, targets=['theta'])
```

with this change, these targets can be safely omitted:

```
        phase.add_state('v', fix_initial=True, fix_final=False, units='m/s', rate_source='vdot')
        phase.add_control(name='theta', units='rad', lower=0, upper=np.pi)
```

The ODE does not take `x` or `y` as inputs so dymos should detect that there is no input of those names and make no connection.

### Environment

N/A

title: Trajectory.add_phase should immediately add the phase instead of queuing it
body:
### Summary of Issue

Trajectory.add_phase should immediately add the phase instead of queuing it.
This will make the phase object's 'name' property available before setup, as it is in most OpenMDAO models.

### Issue Type

- [x] Bug
- [ ] Enhancement

### Description

Expected behavior of OpenMDAO is that a system's `name` property is available after it is added to a subsystem via `add_subsystem`.  Trajectory.add_phase only queues the phase for later addition and breaks this expectation.  add_phase should add the phase-containing subgroup to the trajectory, if not already added, and then add the phase to that system instead of delaying it.

This means the choice of whether a Trajectory runs its phases in a Group or a ParallelGroup will need to be set before the first use of `add_phase`.

### Example

The following code will print the name of the Trajectory, but not the Phase, since it technically hasn't been added to a model yet via `add_subsystem`.

```
import openmdao.api as om
import dymos as dm
p = om.Problem(model=om.Group())
traj = dm.Trajectory()
p.model.add_subsystem('traj', traj)
phase = traj.add_phase('my_phase', dm.Phase())
print(f'traj.name = {traj.name}')
print(f'phase.name = {phase.name}')
```

### Environment

N/A

title: Cyclic constraints
body:
### Summary of Issue

For trajectory optimization of cyclic events (such as race car laps), it would be helpful to be able to define constraints that ensure that the start and end states are identical

### Issue Type

- [] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description

I have been working on trajectory optimization for race cars using Dymos. I would first like to thank you for the great tool that you have put together.

I was wondering if it would be possible to define a boundary constraint that links the initial and final states together. For a cyclic event like a race-car going around a lap I need the states and controls such as velocity, thrust, and steering angle to be the same at the start and finish (see [barca_track_vel_annotated.pdf](https://github.com/OpenMDAO/dymos/files/5133369/barca_track_vel_annotated.pdf) for an example result).

Currently I can do this by manually setting the initial and final values to be the same (fix_initial/fix_final=True) but this is an iterative process. Ideally I would be able to constrain the initial and final values to be the same, but not a fixed value. Is this currently possible in Dymos?

Additionally, I would be glad to provide the problem setup if interested. I am able to find an optimal trajectory for the race car with active aerodynamic and four wheel drive controls.

### Environment

Operating System:  OS X 10.15.5
Python environment: Python 3.8.5
Packages:
dymos @ git+https://github.com/OpenMDAO/dymos.git@5d7e79ab8a89d0c47c3d75aabe299d0a36546fa8

title: Investigate performance issue with multi-trajectory model
body:
### Summary of Issue

User provided the attached model, which gives very weak coloring results and is very slow to converge (about 30 seconds). 


### Issue Type

- [x] Bug
- [ ] Enhancement

### Description

Look for problems in model that cause performance bottleneck, correct any weakness in dymos if found. 


### Example

```
# import libraries
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import *
import sys
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.animation as animation
from matplotlib import pyplot
import time 
import openmdao.api as om
from openmdao.utils.assert_utils import assert_rel_error
import dymos as dm
from dymos.examples.plotting import plot_results 

# ###############################################
# import options and token
n_segments = 25
# N_trajectories = 2 # number of dynamic agents
N_coord = 2 # number of coordinates
number_static_obstacles = 3
number_agents = 8

# Define lower and upper constraints
v_lower = 15.
v_upper = 25.

theta_lower = -25.
theta_upper = 25.

# Define static obstacles
x0_so = np.array([18., 15, 18]) 
y0_so = np.array([16., 15, 18])
so_radius = np.array([3.0, 3.0, 2.0]) 
 
# Define agents
x0_agents = np.array([0.,100.,0.,100.,
                      0.,100, 50., 50.])
xm_agents = np.array([50.,50.,50.,50.,
                      50.,50.,50.,50.])
xf_agents = np.array([100.,0.,100.,0.,
                      100.,0.,50.,50.])

y0_agents = np.array([0.,0.,100.,100., 
                      50.,50.,0.,100.])
ym_agents = np.array([25.,85.,70.,15., 
                      60.,40.,60.,40.])
yf_agents = np.array([100.,100.,0.,0., 
                      50.,50.,100.,0.])

theta_init_agents = np.array([45.,135.,-45.,-135.,
                              0.,-180.,90.,-90.])

x_lower = min(np.concatenate((x0_agents, xf_agents), 
	                          axis=0))-10
x_upper = max(np.concatenate((x0_agents, xf_agents), 
	                          axis=0))+10

y_lower = min(np.concatenate((y0_agents, yf_agents), 
	                          axis=0))-10
y_upper = max(np.concatenate((y0_agents, yf_agents), 
	                          axis=0))+10

 
time_duration_lower = 0.5
time_duration_upper = 20.
time_duration_guess = 100.*np.sqrt(2)/v_upper

agent_radius = np.array([3.0, 3.0, 3.0, 3.0, 
                         3.0, 3.0,3.0,3.0]) 

obj_scaler = 50.

flag_continuity_v = True
flag_rate_continuity_v = False

flag_continuity_theta = True
flag_rate_continuity_theta = False

# ## tokens
token_optimal_solution = 1
token_gif = 1
 
class MinControlSubsystems(om.Group):
    """ 
    Notes:
    """
    def initialize(self):
        self.options.declare('num_nodes', types=int)
        self.options.declare('num_static_obstacles', types=int)
        self.options.declare('num_agents', types=int)     


    def setup(self):
        nn = self.options['num_nodes']  
        nso = self.options['num_static_obstacles']   
        nagents = self.options['num_agents']     

        # subsystem: 2D motion
        for i in range(nagents): 

            self.add_subsystem(name='agent%i_2DmotionODE'%i, 
                               subsys = TwoDimensionalMotionODE(num_nodes=nn)) 
                
            for j in range(nso):

                name_soa_ij = 'agent%i_avoids_static_obstacle%i'% (i,j) 

                self.add_subsystem(name=name_soa_ij,
                                   subsys = StaticObstacleAvoidance(num_nodes=nn))
                # promotes_inputs=['x', 'y'])
            
            set_dynamic_avoidance = np.arange(i+1, nagents)
 
            for k in set_dynamic_avoidance:
                
                # print('agents_inner', i, k)

                name_aaa_ik = 'agent%i_avoids_agent%i'% (i,k)  

                self.add_subsystem(name=name_aaa_ik,
                                   subsys = DynamicObstacleAvoidance(num_nodes=nn))
        
        self.add_subsystem(name='penalize_control', 
                           subsys = PenalizeControl(num_nodes=nn, 
                                                    num_agents=nagents))

# #####################################################    
# #################################################### 
# #################################################### 

class PenalizeControl(om.ExplicitComponent):
    """
    Notes:
    """
    def initialize(self):
        self.options.declare('num_nodes', types=int)
        self.options.declare('num_agents', types=int)

    def setup(self):
        num_nodes = self.options['num_nodes']       
        num_agents = self.options['num_agents']       
        
        for i in range(num_agents):
            # input: v
            self.add_input('agent%i_v'%i, 
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                       desc = 'agent%i_v'%i,
                       units = 'm/s')

            # input: theta
            self.add_input('agent%i_theta'%i, 
                           val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                           desc = 'agent%i_theta'%i,
                           units = 'deg') 
             
            self.add_input('agent%i_x'%i, 
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                       desc = 'agent%i_x'%i,
                       units = 'm')

            # input: theta
            self.add_input('agent%i_y'%i, 
                           val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                           desc = 'agent%i_y'%i,
                           units = 'm') 

        # outputs: d
        self.add_output('penalty_dot',
                        val = np.zeros(num_nodes), 
                        desc='control-penalty-at-a-time',
                        units='1/s')
        
        # Partials
        row_col = np.arange(num_nodes)
        
        for i in range(num_agents):

            self.declare_partials(of='penalty_dot', 
                                  wrt='agent%i_theta'%i, 
                                  rows = row_col,
                                  cols = row_col)

            self.declare_partials(of='penalty_dot', 
                                  wrt='agent%i_v'%i, 
                                  rows = row_col,
                                  cols = row_col)    

            self.declare_partials(of='penalty_dot', 
                                  wrt='agent%i_x'%i, 
                                  rows = row_col,
                                  cols = row_col)

            self.declare_partials(of='penalty_dot', 
                                  wrt='agent%i_y'%i, 
                                  rows = row_col,
                                  cols = row_col)    

    def compute(self, inputs, outputs):       
        num_agents = self.options['num_agents']  
        sum_ux_sq = 0.

        for i in range(num_agents):

            theta_i = inputs['agent%i_theta'%i]
            v_i = inputs['agent%i_v'%i] 
            x_i = inputs['agent%i_x'%i]
            y_i = inputs['agent%i_y'%i]
            sum_ux_sq = sum_ux_sq + theta_i**2 \
                                  + v_i**2 \
                                  + (x_i-xf_agents[i]) ** 2 \
                                  + (y_i-yf_agents[i]) ** 2

        outputs['penalty_dot'] = sum_ux_sq
    

    def compute_partials(self, inputs, partials):
        num_agents = self.options['num_agents']  

        for i in range(num_agents):

            theta_i = inputs['agent%i_theta'%i]
            v_i = inputs['agent%i_v'%i] 
            x_i = inputs['agent%i_x'%i]
            y_i = inputs['agent%i_y'%i]
            # sum_u_sq = sum_u_sq + theta_i**2 + v_i**2

            partials['penalty_dot', 'agent%i_theta'%i] = \
                                        2 * theta_i 
            partials['penalty_dot', 'agent%i_v'%i] = \
                                        2 * v_i 
            partials['penalty_dot', 'agent%i_x'%i] = \
                                        2 * (x_i-xf_agents[i])
            partials['penalty_dot', 'agent%i_y'%i] = \
                                        2 * (y_i-yf_agents[i])               
# ##################################################### 
# #################################################### 
# #################################################### 

class TwoDimensionalMotionODE(om.ExplicitComponent): 

    def initialize(self):
        self.options.declare('num_nodes', types=int)

    def setup(self):
        nn = self.options['num_nodes'] 

        self.add_input('v', val=np.zeros(nn), desc='velocity', 
                       units='m/s') 

        self.add_input('theta', val=np.ones(nn), desc='angle', 
                        units='rad')

        self.add_input('theta_init', val=np.ones(nn), desc='initial angle', 
                        units='rad')        
        # #############
        # outputs
        # #############
        self.add_output('xdot', val=np.zeros(nn), 
                        desc='velocity component in x', units='m/s')

        self.add_output('ydot', val=np.zeros(nn), 
                        desc='velocity component in y', units='m/s') 

        # Setup partials
        arange = np.arange(self.options['num_nodes']) 

        self.declare_partials(of='xdot', wrt='v', rows=arange, cols=arange)
        self.declare_partials(of='xdot', wrt='theta', rows=arange, cols=arange)
        self.declare_partials(of='xdot', wrt='theta_init', rows=arange, cols=arange)

        self.declare_partials(of='ydot', wrt='v', rows=arange, cols=arange)
        self.declare_partials(of='ydot', wrt='theta', rows=arange, cols=arange)
        self.declare_partials(of='ydot', wrt='theta_init', rows=arange, cols=arange) 

    def compute(self, inputs, outputs):
        theta = inputs['theta']
        theta_init = inputs['theta_init']

        cos_the = np.cos(theta_init+theta)
        sin_the = np.sin(theta_init+theta)

        v = inputs['v'] 

        outputs['xdot'] = v * cos_the
        outputs['ydot'] = v * sin_the 

    def compute_partials(self, inputs, jacobian):
        theta = inputs['theta']
        theta_init = inputs['theta_init']

        cos_the = np.cos(theta_init+theta)
        sin_the = np.sin(theta_init+theta)
        
        cthe__thei = -sin_the
        sthe__thei = cos_the
        cthe__the = -sin_the
        sthe__the = cos_the 
        v = inputs['v']  

        jacobian['xdot', 'v'] = cos_the
        jacobian['xdot', 'theta'] = v * cthe__the
        jacobian['xdot', 'theta_init'] = v * cthe__thei

        jacobian['ydot', 'v'] = sin_the
        jacobian['ydot', 'theta'] = v * sthe__the
        jacobian['ydot', 'theta_init'] = v * sthe__thei 

# ##################################################### 
# #################################################### 
# #################################################### 

class DynamicObstacleAvoidance(om.ExplicitComponent):
    """
    Notes:
    """
    def initialize(self):
        self.options.declare('num_nodes', types=int)

    def setup(self):
        num_nodes = self.options['num_nodes']   
        
        # input: x-dyn.obstacle
        self.add_input(name='x_obs', 
                       val = 0.0 * np.ones(num_nodes), 
                       desc='x-coordinate of the dynamic obstacle',
                       units='m')

        # inputs: y-dyn.obstacle
        self.add_input(name='y_obs',
                       val = 0.0 * np.ones(num_nodes),
                       desc='y-coordinate of the dynamic obstacle',
                       units='m')

        # input: x
        self.add_input(name='x', 
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                       desc='x-coordinate',
                       units='m')

        # inputs: y
        self.add_input(name='y',
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),  
                       desc='y-coordinate',
                       units='m')

        # outputs: d
        self.add_output(name='distance',
                        val = np.zeros(num_nodes), 
                        desc='distance from obstacle',
                        units='m**2')

        # Partials
        row_col = np.arange(num_nodes)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='x', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='y', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='x_obs', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='y_obs', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

    def compute(self, inputs, outputs):
        x = inputs['x']
        y = inputs['y']
        x_obs = inputs['x_obs']
        y_obs = inputs['y_obs']

        outputs['distance'] = (x-x_obs)**2 + (y-y_obs)**2 
    
    def compute_partials(self, inputs, partials):
        x = inputs['x']
        y = inputs['y']
        x_obs = inputs['x_obs']
        y_obs = inputs['y_obs']
     
        # d = np.sqrt( (x-5)**2 + (y-5)**2 )

        partials['distance', 'x'] = 2 * (x-x_obs) 
        partials['distance', 'y'] = 2 * (y-y_obs)
        partials['distance', 'x_obs'] = -2 * (x-x_obs) 
        partials['distance', 'y_obs'] = -2 * (y-y_obs)

# ###################################################### 
# ####################################################  

class StaticObstacleAvoidance(om.ExplicitComponent):
    """
    Notes:
    """
    def initialize(self):
        self.options.declare('num_nodes', types=int)

    def setup(self):
        num_nodes = self.options['num_nodes']       

        # input: x
        self.add_input(name='x', 
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                       desc='x-coordinate',
                       units='m')

        # inputs: y
        self.add_input(name='y',
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),  
                       desc='y-coordinate',
                       units='m')

        # input: x
        self.add_input(name='x0', 
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                       desc='x0-coordinate obstacle',
                       units='m')

        # inputs: y
        self.add_input(name='y0',
                       val = np.zeros(num_nodes),
                       desc='y-coordinate obstacle',
                       units='m')

        
        # outputs: d
        self.add_output(name='distance',
                        val = np.zeros(num_nodes), 
                        desc='distance from obstacle',
                        units='m**2')

        # Partials
        row_col = np.arange(num_nodes)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='x', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='y', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='x0', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)

        self.declare_partials(of='distance', wrt='y0', 
                              rows = row_col,
                              cols = row_col)      

    def compute(self, inputs, outputs):
        x = inputs['x']
        y = inputs['y']
        x0 = inputs['x0']
        y0 = inputs['y0']
        outputs['distance'] = (x-x0)**2 + (y-y0)**2 
    
    def compute_partials(self, inputs, partials):
        x = inputs['x']
        y = inputs['y']
        x0 = inputs['x0']
        y0 = inputs['y0']

        partials['distance', 'x'] = 2 * (x-x0) 
        partials['distance', 'y'] = 2 * (y-y0)

        partials['distance', 'x0'] = -2 * (x-x0) 
        partials['distance', 'y0'] = -2 * (y-y0)

# #################################################### 

# #####################################################
p = om.Problem(model=om.Group())
# p.driver = om.ScipyOptimizeDriver()
p.driver = om.pyOptSparseDriver()
p.driver.options['optimizer'] = 'SNOPT' # 'SLSQP'
p.driver.declare_coloring()
p.driver.opt_settings['Major feasibility tolerance'] = 1e-9
p.driver.opt_settings['Major iterations limit'] = 250
# p.driver.options['user_terminate_signal'] = signal.SIGUSR2

token_record=False
if token_record:
    p.driver.add_recorder(om.SqliteRecorder('twodim%d.sql' % n_segments))  
    p.driver.recording_options['includes'] = ['*']
    p.driver.recording_options['record_constraints'] = True
    p.driver.recording_options['record_inputs'] = True
    p.driver.recording_options['record_objectives'] = True
    p.driver.recording_options['record_desvars'] = True
    p.driver.recording_options['record_responses'] = True
    p.driver.recording_options['record_derivatives'] = True

# add trajectory
traj = p.model.add_subsystem('traj', dm.Trajectory())

phase = traj.add_phase('phase0', dm.Phase(ode_class=MinControlSubsystems,
                                          ode_init_kwargs={'num_static_obstacles': number_static_obstacles, 
                                                           'num_agents': number_agents}, 
                                          transcription=dm.GaussLobatto(num_segments=n_segments) 
                                          ) 
                       )

# #########################3# #########################
phase.set_time_options(initial_bounds=(0, 0), 
                       duration_bounds=(time_duration_lower, time_duration_upper),
                       units = 's') #targets = 'time')

# ###################################################
for i in range(number_agents):
    
    target_x, target_y = [], []
    target_x_aa, target_y_aa = [], []

    for j in range(number_static_obstacles):

        target_x__ij = 'agent%i_avoids_static_obstacle%i.x'% (i,j)
        target_x.append(target_x__ij)

        target_y__ij = 'agent%i_avoids_static_obstacle%i.y'% (i,j)
        target_y.append(target_y__ij)

    set_dynamic_avoidance = np.arange(i+1, number_agents)
    
    for k in set_dynamic_avoidance:

        target_x_ij = 'agent%i_avoids_agent%i.x'% (i,k)
        target_x.append(target_x_ij)

        target_y_ij = 'agent%i_avoids_agent%i.y'% (i,k)
        target_y.append(target_y_ij)
    
    set_dynamic_avoidance = np.arange(0, i)
    
    for k in set_dynamic_avoidance:

        target_x_ij = 'agent%i_avoids_agent%i.x_obs'% (k,i)
        target_x.append(target_x_ij)

        target_y_ij = 'agent%i_avoids_agent%i.y_obs'% (k,i)
        target_y.append(target_y_ij)

    target_x.append('penalize_control.agent%i_x'%i)
    target_y.append('penalize_control.agent%i_y'%i)

    phase.add_state('agent%i_x'%i, 
                    rate_source='agent%i_2DmotionODE.xdot'%i,
                    targets=target_x, 
                    units='m', 
                    lower = x_lower, upper = x_upper,
                    fix_initial=True, fix_final=True, solve_segments=False)        
    
    phase.add_state('agent%i_y'%i,

title: Controls now automatically connected to top-level ODE inputs of same name if present
body:
# Summary

This PR enables automatic targeting of control variables.
If left unspecified, a control will attempt to target a top-level input of the ODE if it has the same name.

Using automatic state/control targets currently breaks grid refinement, which has exposed a hole in our testing.

### Related Issues

Resolves #366 
Resolves #318 

### Status

- [x] Ready for merge

### Backwards incompatibilities

Previously, the user was required to explicitly connect variables (time, states, controls, polynomial controls, or parameters) to ODE inputs.
Now, if left unspecified, Dymos will connect those variables to a top-level ODE input of the same name, if present.
There's a small chance that these automatic connections will be made in ways that weren't intended.
To disable automatic connection to the ODE, the targets should be set to `None`.
The deprecation warning regarding variables automatically targeting top-level ODE inputs of the same name have been removed.

### New Dependencies

None

Previously, when an ODE output was added as a timeseries output variable, the units and shape had to be specified as well. (a shape of (1,) was assumed if not given). Gets the shape and units of a given variable target in an ODE.  If multiple targets exist, then the shape and units are required to be the same across all targets.  Otherwise, the user must manually specify them.

title: add_timeseries_output should allow multiple variables to be added per call
body:
### Summary of Issue

Large models can require numerous calls to `add_timeseries_output`.
Recent changes to dymos now allow it to infer the shape and units of all outputs, including ODE outputs.
Now, to further reduce the amount of input required from a user, add_timeseries_output should allow multiple variables to be specified in a single call.

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description and Examples

The following uses of add_timeseries_output should be legal:

1. Wildcards

`add_timeseries_output('*')` will add all outputs from the ODE to the timeseries outputs

`add_timeseries_output('aero.*')` will add all outputs from an ODE subsystem named `aero` to the timeseries outputs.

2. Multiple outputs

`add_timeseries_output(['CD', 'CL']) would add variables named CD and CL to the timeseries outputs.

In the case of adding multiple outputs in a single call, the units option should accept either strings or dictionaries.

`add_timeseries_output(['m_dry', 'm_fuel'])` would add those two variables with their units inferred from the ODE outputs

3. Units

`add_timeseries_output(['m_dry', 'm_fuel'], units='lbm')` would add those two variables with units of lbm, and attempt the unit  conversion for both.

`add_timeseries_output(['m_dry', 'm_fuel', 'force_lift'], units='lbm')` would attempt to assign lbm to all 3 outputs, but should fail assuming `force_lift` is defined with units of force and not mass.

`add_timeseries_output(['m_dry', 'm_fuel', 'force_lift'], units={'m_dry': 'lbm', 'm_fuel': 'lbm', 'force_lift:lbf')` would would explicitly define units for all outputs.  

It should also be legal to explicitly provide units for some outputs.

`add_timeseries_output(['m_dry', 'm_fuel', 'force_lift'], units={'m_dry': 'lbm', 'm_fuel': 'lbm')`, where `force_lift` has its units automatically determined.

`add_timeseries_output('aero.*', units={'force_lift': 'lbf'})` would be legal but raise an exception if force_lift isn't found during the wildcard expansion.

N/A

### Summary of Issue

Tweak the functionality of `run_problem`

### Issue Type

- [ ] Bug
- [x] Enhancement

### Description and Examples

1. The `refine` argument is redundant with `refine_iteration_limit`.  Simply using `refine_iteration_limit < 0` should have the same effect, and we can remove the refine argument (with deprecation warning until 1.0.0).

2. Refinement should not happen if run_driver is False.

3. The entire grid_refinement loop should be moved to a function under grid_refinement.

4. The record file names for the problem solution recording and the simulation recording should be arguments to run_problem.  The default for simulation should be `dymos_simulation.db` and for the solution it should be `dymos_solution.db`.

5. Add an argument `load_case` to specify the filename from which to load a previous solution.

### Sequence of Events

1. Run final_setup on the problem so that command line hooks will trigger.
2. If a restart file is provided (a recorded file from a previous solution or simulate call) then load values from that into the problem.
3. run_driver if desired, otherwise run_model
4. begin the refinement loop, if refinement is enabled
5. Run simulate on the solution, if directed to do so.
